'''Joseph A. Sgro''' (born in [[San Diego]], California) is an American [[mathematician]], [[neurologist]] / [[neurophysiologist]], and an [[engineering technologist]] / [[entrepreneur]] in the field of [[frame grabber]]s, [[high-speed camera]]s, [[smart camera]]s, [[image processor]]s, [[computer vision]], and [[machine vision]] and [[machine learning|learning]] technologies.

Sgro began his career as an academic researcher in advanced mathematics and logic.  He received an AB in mathematics in 1970 from [[University of California, Los Angeles|UCLA]] followed by an MA in mathematics in 1973 and a PhD in mathematics in 1975 from the [[University of Wisconsin]], where he studied [[mathematical logic]] under [[Howard Jerome Keisler|H. Jerome Keisler]]<ref>[[Mathematics Genealogy Project]] entry for [http://genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=9322 Joseph A. Sgro].</ref> who along with [[Jon Barwise]] and [[Kenneth Kunen]] formed his doctoral committee.

After serving as an instructor and postdoctoral fellow at [[Yale University]] and also was a member of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]], Sgro returned to school to study neurology, and received his M.D. in 1980 from the Ph.D to M.D. Program<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1097/ACM.0b013e3181d296da |title=Perspective: PhD Scientists Completing Medical School in Two Years: Looking at the Miami PhD-to-MD Program Alumni Twenty Years Later |year=2010 |last1=Koniaris |first1=Leonidas G. |last2=Cheung |first2=Michael C. |last3=Garrison |first3=Gwen |last4=Awad Jr |first4=William M. |last5=Zimmers |first5=Teresa A. |journal=Academic Medicine |volume=85 |issue=4 |pages=687–91 |pmid=20354390|doi-access=free }}</ref> of the [[Miller School of Medicine]] at the [[University of Miami]], followed by an internal medicine internship at [[UNC Health Care|UNC Memorial Hospital]], residency in [[neurology]], a fellowship, and faculty position in [[clinical neurophysiology]] at the [[Neurological Institute of New York]].

As an outgrowth of his work in neurophysiology, while still working as a postdoctoral fellow and an assistant professor of neurology, Sgro founded Alacron, Inc., formerly Corteks, Inc. until 1990, in 1985 to manufacture technologies relevant to his neurological research. In 1989, he commercialized this technology and began developing [[array processor]]s, frame grabbers, vision processors, and most recently supported advances in [[Backside illumination|BSI]] and superlattice (delta) sensor doping<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hoenk |first1=Michael |title=Surface passivation by quantum exclusion using multiple layers |url=http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO1&Sect2=HITOFF&d=PALL&p=1&u=%2Fnetahtml%2FPTO%2Fsrchnum.htm&r=1&f=G&l=50&s1=9024344.PN.&OS=PN/9024344&RS=PN/9024344 |website=USPTO |access-date=7 September 2020}}</ref> technology.  Extending his work in machine vision technology, in 2002, Sgro founded FastVision, LLC, a maker of [[smart camera]]s, as a subsidiary of Alacron, Inc . In 2016, FastVision, LLC. was incorporated into Alacron, Inc.

==Mathematical research==
During his first year as a PhD candidate at the University of Wisconsin, Sgro proved that a [[topological]] extension of [[first-order logic]] using the [[open set]] logic [[Quantifier (logic)|quantifier]] has [[completeness (logic)|logical completeness]], which had previously been widely believed but had not been proven. Sgro's proof drew attention throughout mathematical world, and, in 1974, a year before finishing his PhD, he was awarded an appointment as a Josiah Willard Gibbs Instructor in Mathematics at Yale University, received an [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] research grant to continue his work in topological model theory.<ref>"Topological Model Theory," [https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward.do?AwardNumber=7704131 National Science Foundation, Division of Mathematical Sciences, award number 77-04131], 1977</ref>  Yale allowed him to accept this honor while remotely completing his thesis and dissertation at Wisconsin, which he did in 1975.  His conclusions regarding the topological model theory formed the basis of his PhD thesis and dissertation. During the 1976–1977 academic year Sgro received a Centennial Fellowship<ref>Centennial Fellowship [https://www.ams.org/about-us/governance/committees/centfellow-charge.pdf Overview and Roster]</ref> from the [[American Mathematical Society|AMS]].  His work also resulted in an invitation to speak at the Logica Colloquim ’77 European Meeting of the [[Association for Symbolic Logic]].  This event was held in [[Wrocław]], [[Poland]], which was then still part of the [[Eastern Bloc]], making Sgro among the first mathematicians from the West to speak at an event “behind the Iron Curtain.”<ref>Logic Colloquium ’77, Wroclaw, Poland.  Macintyre, A., L. Pacholski, J. Paris, eds.  In Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics, Volume 96.  Barwise, J., D. Kaplan, H. J. Keisler, et al., series eds.  North-Holland Publishing Company, 1978.  {{ISBN|0-444-85178-X}}.</ref>  Sgro also spent 1977–1978 at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in Princeton, New Jersey.<ref>Institute for Advanced Study membership roster entry for [http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/users/jsgro01 Joseph A. Sgro] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140506215117/http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/users/jsgro01 |date=2014-05-06 }}</ref>

Published in 1977, Sgro's thesis “Completeness Theorems for Topological Models”<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/0003-4843(77)90016-X |volume=11 |issue=2 |title=Completeness theorems for topological models |journal=Annals of Mathematical Logic |pages=173–193 |year=1977 |last1=Sgro |first1=Joseph|doi-access= }}</ref> and extensions of this research including the [[axiomatization]] and completeness of [[continuous function]]s on [[product topology]] open set quantifiers was published in 1976 in the [[Israel Journal of Mathematics]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Completeness theorems for continuous functions and product topologies |first=Joseph |last=Sgro |date=1 September 1976 |journal=[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]] |volume=25 |issue=3–4 |pages=249–272 |doi=10.1007/BF02757004|doi-access=|s2cid=119532738 }}</ref> Following these results, Sgro published a proof that an extension of the open set quantifier logic using [[interior operator]] quantifier logic has completeness and satisfies [[Craig interpolation]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1980-258-01/S0002-9947-1980-0554321-4/S0002-9947-1980-0554321-4.pdf |title=The interior operator logic and product topologies }}</ref>  He further showed that the Souslin-Kleene closure<ref>{{cite journal |title=Axioms for abstract model theory |first=K. |last=Jon Barwise |date=1 December 1974 |journal=Annals of Mathematical Logic |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=221–265 |doi=10.1016/0003-4843(74)90016-3|doi-access= }}</ref>  of the open set quantifier logic fails Craig Interpolation which implies that it is strictly weaker than the interior operator logic.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1980-078-04/S0002-9939-1980-0556634-4/S0002-9939-1980-0556634-4.pdf |title=Interpolation fails for the Souslin-Kleene closure of the open-set quantifier logic }}</ref> His later research concentrated on proving the existence of maximal extensions of first order logic which satisfy [[Łoś's theorem]] on [[ultraproduct]]s and have the Souslin-Kleene property.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1977-063-02/S0002-9939-1977-0491143-2/S0002-9939-1977-0491143-2.pdf |title=Maximal Logics }}</ref>  Also this was extended to ultraproduct extensions of first order logic which satisfied both the Łoś's theorem and an extended form of the [[compactness theorem]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1980-079-04/S0002-9939-1980-0572318-0/S0002-9939-1980-0572318-0.pdf |title=Ultraproduct invariant logic }}</ref>

==Neurological research==

While researching mathematical logic, Sgro became interested in investigating the logic systems that the brain uses to process motor and sensory information, and returned to school, intending to study clinical neurophysiology, the branch of [[neurology]] and [[physiology]] that examines the functioning of the peripheral and central [[nervous system]]. Neurophysiological research typically uses imaging tools for visualizing chemical and electrical activity in nerve pathways, and today includes [[Functional magnetic resonance imaging|fMRI]], [[electroencephalography]] (EEG), [[evoked potentials]] (EPs), [[transcranial magnetic stimulation|TMS]] and other technologies to visualize and evaluate brain activity.

After Sgro completed his [[internship]] in [[internal medicine]] at the [[University of North Carolina]] in 1981 and his [[Residency (medicine)|residency]] in neurology at [[Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center]] in 1984. Sgro served as a [[post-doctoral fellow]] in clinical neurophysiology (1983–1985), as an Associate in Neurology (1985–1986) and then as an [[assistant professor]] of neurology (1986–1987) at The [[Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons|College of Physicians and Surgeons]] at [[Columbia University]] in [[New York City]].  Sgro relocated to [[Richmond, Virginia]], where he was an [[associate professor]] of neurology and the head of neurophysiology (1987–1991) and finally, as Chief of the Division of Clinical Neurophysiology (1991–1994) at the [[VCU Medical Center|Virginia Commonwealth University Medical Center]].  He was also appointed as an adjunct associate professor of neurology at [[Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center]] from 1994 until 2004.

During his postdoctoral fellowship at [[Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center]], Sgro achieved recognition in the medical community for his research and findings on the theory of [[evoked potentials]], with a particular focus on [[Somatosensory Evoked Potential]]s (SSEPs).  A summary of Sgro's efforts to improve evoked potential recording recording technology is found in Keith Chiappa's book.<ref name="auto">Sgro, J. A., R. G. Emerson, and P. C. Stanton. "Advanced techniques of evoked potential acquisition and processing."''Evoked Potentials in Clinical Medicine. 3rd ed. Philadelphia: Lippincott-Raven'' (1997): 579-600. {{ISBN|978-0397516599}}</ref> This article covers many one and two [[dimensional]], [[linear]] and [[non-linear]] [[digital filter]]s.  Two approaches to improve recording fidelity is by increasing the [[signal-to-noise ratio]]  (SNR) by the reduction of coherent [[electrical]] [[noise]]<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/0013-4694(85)91021-1 |pmid=2580698 |volume=60 |issue=5 |title=Phase synchronized triggering: A method for coherent noise elimination in evoked potential recording |journal=Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology |pages=464–468 |year=1985 |last1=Sgro |first1=Joseph A. |last2=Emerson |first2=Ronald G.}}</ref>  and second the development of a two dimensional [[Discrete Fourier transform|DFT]] digital filtering of evoked potentials which trades off the SNR improvement of the [[moving average]] technique with the detection of changes in the averaged [[waveform]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/0168-5597(85)90046-2 |pmid=2411519 |volume=62 |issue=5 |title=Real-time reconstruction of evoked potentials using a new two-dimensional filter method |journal= Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology/Evoked Potentials Section|pages=372–380 |year=1985 |last1=Sgro |first1=Joseph A. |last2=Emerson |first2=Ronald G. |last3=Pedley |first3=Timothy A.}}</ref>  Using this technology, Sgro proved that SSEPs were “state dependent,” varying depending on whether the patient was [[awake]] or [[asleep]] ([[anesthetized]]).<ref name="auto1">{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/0920-1211(93)90095-O |pmid=8370352 |volume=15 |issue=2 |title=Conventional and rapid stimulation evoked potential changes in patients with status epilepticus |journal=Epilepsy Research |pages=149–156 |year=1993 |last1=Sgro |first1=Joseph A. |last2=Jaitly |first2=Rakesh |last3=Delorenzo |first3=Robert J.|s2cid=11714485 }}</ref>  Following these findings with funding from the [[Whitaker Foundation]],<ref>''The Development of Methods for the Analysis of Non-Time-Stable Brain Responses.'' Whitaker Foundation grant, 1985-1989</ref> Sgro developed technology and techniques to analyze evoked potentials based on stimulation run by an ultra fast (i.e. hundreds of [[hertz]]) [[pseudorandom m-sequence]]s.<ref name="auto"/><ref>{{cite web |author=Jens Hee |url=http://jenshee.dk/signalprocessing/mls.pdf |title=Impulse response measurements using MLS |website=jenshee.dk |date=August 2003 |access-date=2017-06-23}}</ref><ref>Marmarmelis, P. and Marmarmelis, V.Z., Analysis of PhysiologicalSystem, Plenum Press, New York, NY, 1978.</ref>  This work was demonstrated to be a more effective method of identification and predictor of sub-clinical diseases or damage such as [[Death|mortality]] from [[status epilepticus]]<ref name="auto1"/><ref>[https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/projectreporter.nih.gov/project_info_description.cfm?aid=3901794 "Assessment of Afferent and Efferent Neuropathways in Severe Head Injury," NIH Program Project Grant #2P01NS012587, 1989-1992.].</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/projectreporter.nih.gov/project_info_description.cfm?aid=3902216 |title=Project Information - NIH RePORTER - NIH Research Portfolio Online Reporting Tools Expenditures and Results |first=metatags |last=generator |website=projectreporter.nih.gov}}</ref> (diseases that otherwise went undetected until they become severe enough to qualify as clinically apparent when compared to conventional evoked potentials).

While conducting research into the (afferent) [[sensory nervous system]] with evoked potentials, Sgro also began to investigate devices and techniques to determine the state of the (efferent) [[motor system|motor nervous system]] using [[transcranial magnetic stimulation|TMS]] with the goal of more effective detection of sub-clinical diseases and increased sensitivity of the motor system during intra-operative patient monitoring. Sgro<ref>{{Cite journal |pmid = 1773765|year = 1991|last1 = Sgro|first1 = J.|title = Theoretical and practical performance of magnetic stimulators and coils|journal = Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology. Supplement|volume = 43|pages = 279–83|last2 = Stanton|first2 = P.|last3 = Emerson|first3 = R.}}</ref> and his associates studied the theoretical and practical issues involved in the design of a high magnetic field strength and rapid transcranial magnetic stimulator which could exceed the historical safety limit of [[electrical brain stimulation]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Agnew |first1=WF |last2=McCreery |first2=DB |year=1987 |title=Considerations for safety in the use of extracranial stimulation for motor evoked potentials |journal=Neurosurgery |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=143–7 |doi=10.1097/00006123-198701000-00030 |pmid=3808255}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Agnew |first1=WF |last2=Yuen |first2=TG |last3=McCreery |first3=DB |year=1983 |title=Morphologic changes after prolonged electrical stimulation of the cat's cortex at defined charge densities |journal=Exp Neurol |volume=79 |issue=2 |pages=397–411 |doi=10.1016/0014-4886(83)90221-2 |pmid=6822271|s2cid=37339997 }}</ref> (40 uC/cm2/phase at a stimulation rate of 20 to 50 Hertz over several hours).  These studies resulted in the construction of a rapid high magnetic field strength device<ref>{{cite web |url=http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO1&Sect2=HITOFF&d=PALL&p=1&u=/netahtml/PTO/srchnum.htm&r=1&f=G&l=50&s1=5,061,234.PN.&OS=PN/5,061,234&RS=PN/5,061,234 |title=United States Patent: 5061234 - Magnetic neural stimulator for neurophysiology }}</ref> which was suitable for safety studies.  The safety of TMS in rats with a maximal field strength of 3.4 [[Tesla (unit)|tesla]] at 8 Herz for 20 minutes or 10uC/cm2/phase was demonstrated in Sgro<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sgro |first1=J A |last2=Ghatak |first2=N R |last3=Stanton |first3=P C |last4=Emerson |first4=R G |last5=Blair |first5=R |year=1991 |title=Repetitive high magnetic field stimulation: the effect upon rat brain |journal=Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology. Supplement |volume=43 |pages=180–5 |pmid=1773756}}</ref>

While working as a neurology researcher Sgro began work in [[biomedical engineering]] and machine vision, specifically the use of imaging and machine vision technologies, to assess the function and integrity of the [[nervous system]] in various states of [[consciousness]], during [[medical procedures]], and disease.  The research was performed initially using [[computer program]]s written in [[Fortran]] running on a [[Digital Equipment Corporation|DEC]] [[Programmed Data Processor|PDP]] [[minicomputer]].  In the mid 1980s the widespread adoption of [[IBM PC compatible]] computers with the [[Industry Standard Architecture|ISA]] bus enabled the development of [[personal computer|PC]] based [[expansion cards]] to increase the functionality of the PC. To facilitate lower cost advanced hardware development, Sgro co-founded Alacron, Inc. to develop advanced [[medical research]] equipment and commercial PC based products.

During the mid 1990s, Sgro began to study the use of [[artificial intelligence]] methods in the automation of neurophysiological monitoring.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sgro |first1=Joseph |title=Neural network classification of clinical neurophysiological data for acute care monitoring |journal=JPL, A Decade of Neural Networks: Practical Applications and Prospects |date=11 May 1994|url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19950018843%202019-05-30T21:09:35%2000:00 |access-date=10 September 2020}}</ref>  Sgro conducted research into the use of [[backpropagation]] [[artificial neural networks|neural networks]] in clinical monitoring and automatic neurophysiological interpretation of EEG and evoked potentials. An overview of this approach to evoked potentials was outlined in<ref>{{cite book |last1=Sgro |first1=J. A. |last2=Emerson |first2=R. G. |last3=Stanton |first3=P. C. |title=1998 IEEE International Joint Conference on Neural Networks Proceedings. IEEE World Congress on Computational Intelligence (Cat. No.98CH36227) |chapter=Automated evoked potential analysis using backpropagation networks |date=4–9 May 1998 |volume=1 |pages=123–127 |doi=10.1109/IJCNN.1998.682248 |isbn=0-7803-4859-1 |s2cid=57323507 }}</ref> where it was shown in a pilot study that using a multiple hidden layer neural network, e.g.[[deep learning]], the classification and latency [[measurement]]s of visual, [[Brainstem auditory evoked potential|brainstem auditory]], and somatosensory [[evoked potential]]s is comparable to human expert classification.  Additional research<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sgro |first1=J.A. |last2=Emerson |first2=R.G. |last3=Stanton |first3=P.C. |title=Automated EEG classification by neural networks |journal=Proceedings of the International Conference on Imaging Science, Systems, and Technology |date=6–9 July 1998 |pages=295–301 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/308787418 |access-date=9 September 2020}}</ref>  into the [[machine learning]] of EEG using Higher-Order Neural Networks (HONN)<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Giles |first1=C.L. |last2=Griffin |first2=R.D. |last3=Maxwell |first3=T. |title=Encoding geometric invariances in higher order neural networks |journal=NIPS |date=1987 |url=http://papers.nips.cc/paper/14-encoding-geometric-invariances-in-higher-order-neural-networks.pdf |access-date=10 September 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Goggin |first1=Shelly |last2=Johnson |first2=Kristina |last3=Gustafson |first3=Karl|author3-link=Karl Edwin Gustafson |title=A second-order translation, rotation and scale invariant neural network |journal=NIPS |date=1991 |pages=313–319 |url=http://papers.nips.cc/paper/362-a-second-order-translation-rotation-and-scale-invariant-neural-network.pdf |access-date=10 September 2020}}</ref> also produced comparable results when compared to human expert classification.

==Entrepreneurial career==

===Alacron, Inc.===

In 1985, Sgro co-founded [http://www.alacron.com Alacron, Inc.] in [[Nashua, New Hampshire]].  Sgro and the Alacron engineering team focused on the development and production of [[frame grabber]]s and high speed image processing computational subsystems.  The product family currently includes frame grabbers, software, data recording devices and supporting peripherals. Despite initial focus on neurophysiology research and medical imaging, Alacron saw uses for its products expand outside the field of medicine into other applications, such as manufacturing, military, and other industries that use robotics extensively.  Alacron is one of the largest frame grabber manufacturers in the [[Automated Imaging Association]]'s annual market data report.<ref>[http://www.machinevisiononline.org/market-data.cfm?id=100 Automated Imaging Association annual market data report overview]. Membership in AIA is required to obtain full report.</ref>

Examples of broader machine vision uses of frame grabbers originally developed for use in medical imaging include [[American Science and Engineering|AS&E]], which incorporated Alacron technology in [[backscatter X-ray]] equipment used for border security, and as image capture used for [[Voyage Data Recorder]]s, the maritime equivalent of aviation “[[Flight recorder|black box]]es.”

In addition to the commercial product lines offered by Alacron, Sgro continued to perform basic research in integrating frame grabber technology with specialized systems for various disciplines.  The company received [[Small Business Innovation Research|SBIR]] grants where Sgro acted as principal investigators, including:

*"A Digital Signal Processing Evoked Potential Machine” [[National Institutes of Health|NIH]] SBIR #1R44NS024494. 1986 (Phase 1), 1988-1990 (Phase 2).<ref>[https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/projectreporter.nih.gov/project_info_description.cfm?aid=3509178 "A Digital Signal Processing Evoked Potential Machine"], [[National Institutes of Health|NIH]] SBIR #1R44NS024494, 1986.</ref>
*"A Self Optimizing Evoked Potential Amplifier,” NIH SBIR #1R43NS24490.  1986-1987  (Phase 1), 1989-1991 (Phase 2).<ref>[https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/projectreporter.nih.gov/project_info_description.cfm?aid=3509175 "A Self Optimizing Evoked Potential Amplifier," NIH SBIR #2R44NS024490, 1986-1991].</ref>
*"A Magnetic Stimulator for Neurophysiology," NIH SBIR #1R43NS24924, 1986-1987 (Phase 1); 1989-1991 (Phase 2).
*"An Event Detecting Video/EEG Monitoring System," NlH SBIR #1R43NS26204, 1988–1989.
*"A Magnetic Neural Stimulator for Neurophysiology," NIH SBIR II #2R44NS24924, 1989–1991.<ref>[https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/projectreporter.nih.gov/project_info_description.cfm?aid=3509190 "A Magnetic Neural Stimulator for Neurophysiology," NIH SBIR II #2R44NS24924, 1989-1991].</ref>
*”An Efficient Lossless EEG Compression Engine,” NIH SBIR #1R43NS34211.  1995-1997 (phase 1); 1999-2003 (phase 2).<ref>[https://reporter.nih.gov/project-details/projectreporter.nih.gov/project_info_description.cfm?aid=6013357 "An Efficient Lossless EEG Compression Engine," NIH SBIR #1R43NS34211, 1995-2003].</ref>
*"Scalable Programmable Accelerator for Affordable High Performance Computing," [[DARPA]] Contract #N66001-96-C-8611, 1997–2001.

Academic presentations of Alacron's technology and research include: 
*"[http://ca.pittcon.org/Technical+Program/TPAbstra06.nsf/Agenda+Time+Slots+Web/5DEC35AC30EA3FC98525708A004EBDED?Opendocument&showclose&rnd=0.5Machine Vision Solutions for Life Sciences Applications]" at [[Pittsburgh Conference on Analytical Chemistry and Applied Spectroscopy|Pittcon]], 2006.<ref>[http://ca.pittcon.org/Technical+Program/TPAbstra06.nsf/Agenda+Time+Slots+Web/5DEC35AC30EA3FC98525708A004EBDED?Opendocument&showclose&rnd=0.5 Machine Vision Solutions for Life Sciences Applications] at [[Pittsburgh Conference on Analytical Chemistry and Applied Spectroscopy|Pittcon]], 2006.</ref>

===FastVision, LLC===

In 2002, Sgro launched [http://www.fast-vision.com FastVision, LLC].  FastVision builds high-speed megapixel-plus digital cameras, based on [[CMOS sensor|CMOS]] and [[Charge-coupled device|CCD]] image sensors . The company's goal is to produce [[smart camera]]s, i.e. cameras with high-speed scalable integrated [[image processing]] capabilities built into the same package housing the opto-electronics.  Like most smart camera vendors, FastVision's suite includes [[Field-programmable gate array|FPGA]] processing and memory subsystems to enable in-camera image processing. When integrated with a high powered frame grabber or vision processor board (or a host subsystem), the resulting system capabilities can be expanded beyond simple image compression.  The smart camera subsystem can be integrated with disk or non-volatile semiconductor storage inside or outside the camera to hold sustained real-time data acquisition, a valuable aid to system effectiveness when network connectivity is overloaded or is unavailable.

Applications for smart cameras range from security and surveillance, to robotics in medicine and manufacturing, to military applications such as bots, drones and intelligent weaponry, to satellites and inner and outer space exploration.
